candidates.title: Robust Parameter-Efficient LLM Adaptation on Analog Hardware
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Analog in-memory computing is a promising platform for on-device execution of large language models because it performs matrix--vector multiplications (MVMs) in memory and in parallel, reducing data movement. However, limited digital-to-analog converter precision, input noise, and finite conductance states can degrade model accuracy, while full-model retraining to address these effects can be costly. We develop an optimizer-agnostic, parameter-efficient adaptation method based on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), keeping the pretrained weights stored on analog arrays fixed while training the LoRA weights to adapt to downstream tasks and hardware non-idealities. Reliable adaptation requires handling errors in both forward and backward MVMs and physical weight updates. We use input reshaping to reduce input-induced MVM errors and update accumulation to retain small updates before programming them to finite-state analog devices. Across Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Llama-3-8B with both Muon and AdamW, input reshaping improves analog LoRA fine-tuning under noisy MVM computation. candidates.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. candidates.title: A Fine-Grained Analysis of the LoRA Fine-Tuning Landscape with Implications for Data Selection
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. Our central insight is that the appropriate adapter rank should depend on the quality of the data-induced optimization geometry, rather than on the model alone. candidates.title: FedLore: Communication and Memory Efficient Federated Learning via Shared Gradient Low-Rank Projection
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Federated training of foundation models is constrained by client memory and communication costs. LoRA-based methods reduce these costs through low-rank adapters, but their fixed rank budget can limit adaptation. Gradient low-rank optimization offers greater flexibility, yet independently chosen client subspaces create a problem we term \emph{subspace fragmentation}: local projections interact with data heterogeneity to bias aggregated directions, while aggregation can increase update rank and communication cost. Thus, accurate local gradient compression need not preserve global descent. We propose \texttt{FedLore}, which shares a low-rank optimization basis within each round and refreshes it across rounds. The shared basis enables exact aggregation in low-rank coordinates and eliminates the identified projection bias. Subspace refresh allows the accumulated model update to exceed the per-round rank budget. candidates.title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. candidates.title: LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. candidates.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. candidates.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. candidates.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3\% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. candidates.title: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified \textit{margin-based perspective}. We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with $\ell_2$-regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the \emph{max-margin solution} on the fine-tuning data. candidates.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.

candidates.title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. candidates.title: Optimizer Geometry Sets the Pace: Spectral Learning Dynamics in Matrix Factorization
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. candidates.title: Spectrally Targeted Muon
candidates.abstract_excerpt: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. candidates.title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.

candidates.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. candidates.title: LoRA's Second Descent Extends Beyond Parameter Parity
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter's rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Spectral weight decay lowers the effective rank of weight matrices, making them amenable to low-rank compression. We use SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , which gives the lowest validation loss in our matched comparison. We compress each weight matrix to its own effective rank, which varies substantially across layers (Figure 2 , middle). We leave the token embeddings and output head uncompressed because their ranks respond little to spectral weight decay, and compressing them even to their effective ranks sharply degrades model quality. The comparison and compression procedure are described in Appendix B.4 . Figure 3 (top) reports the maximum compression rate supported by each validation-loss distortion budget. Spectral weight decay substantially shifts this frontier upward at all three model scales. For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. The same factorization reduces the FLOPs of a linear layer when r ⁡ ( m + n ) < m ​ n r(m+n)<mn . The additional kernel launch and intermediate activation can offset the reduction in FLOPs. To improve tensor-core utilization, we round the effective rank down to the nearest multiple of 16 16 , r l = max ⁡ ( 16 , 16 ​ ⌊ erank ⁡ ( W l ) 16 ⌋ ) , r_{l}=\max\!\left(16,\,16\left\lfloor\frac{\operatorname{erank}(W_{l})}{16}\right\rfloor\right), (3)

Adjusting an aligned rank by one step, ± 16 \pm 16 , has negligible effect on validation loss. We therefore use this rank-aligned compression scheme throughout. The factorized models outperform their dense counterparts only at large batch sizes, so we measure forward-pass latency with a batch size of 256 256 on a single GPU. For the 500 500 M model, spectral weight decay yields a 1.09 × 1.09\times speedup near a 2 % 2\% distortion budget and reaches 1.18 × 1.18\times at 4 % 4\% , compared with 1.01 × 1.01\times under standard weight decay (Figure 3 , bottom).

2610.23571:98d9bb351aa95d1114b5d3f302d91.question: What model-quality and structured-pruning results does BMuon report for language models versus Muon at matched training settings, and what training or compression costs are measured?

passages.text: Modern Transformer models incur substantial memory and computational costs at inference time, motivating compression for more efficient deployment ( Kwon et al., 2022 ) . Pruning is a natural approach to this problem, but practical gains depend on the sparsity structure: unstructured sparsity often requires specialized kernels or hardware, whereas structured pruning removes entire computational units and translates directly into efficiency gains ( Wen et al., 2016 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Feed-forward modules can account for roughly two thirds of Transformer parameters ( Geva et al., 2021 ) , making their hidden channels a natural target for structured compression. Global pruning ranks channels across layers jointly, allowing different layers to retain different numbers of channels ( Lee et al., 2021 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Post-pruning fine-tuning adds computational cost, especially for large models ( Kwon et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) , motivating compressibility to emerge during training so that pruning requires little or no recovery. Figure 1 : Post-training global MLP pruning on ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16. Mean ± \pm std over 3 seeds. See Appendix E.1 .

Muon has demonstrated strong training efficiency across model scales, from small vision and language-model benchmarks to billion-parameter language models ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) . Its matrix update can be viewed as a linear minimization oracle over a spectral-norm ball, giving Muon a steepest-descent interpretation in spectral-norm geometry ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) . Prior work has shown that implicit bias can depend on optimization geometry ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) . For Muon, recent theory identifies a spectral-norm margin bias in linear and smooth homogeneous models ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Gronich and Vardi, 2026 ) . Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers degrade rapidly under structured MLP pruning, suggesting that Muon’s spectral geometry does not by itself encourage structured compressibility. As shown in Figure 1 , a Muon-trained ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K collapses after only 30 % 30\% global MLP channel pruning, with Top-1 accuracy falling from 75.23 % 75.23\% to 3.17 % 3.17\% . In contrast, our proposed Budget Muon (BMuon) algorithm retains 74.08 % 74.08\% Top-1 accuracy after 70 % 70\% pruning, nearly matching its 74.17 % 74.17\% accuracy before pruning, with no post-pruning recovery. This raises the central question: can Muon’s spectral geometry be modified to encourage structured compressibility?

To address this question, we introduce BMuon, which reweights Muon’s spectral geometry under a single global budget K K shared across all hidden channels of all MLP blocks. For hidden channel j j in block ℓ \ell , BMuon assigns an allocation μ j ℓ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mu_{j}^{\ell}\in[0,1] to the corresponding row of the up-projection matrix and column of the down-projection matrix, with ∑ ℓ , j μ j ℓ = K \sum_{\ell,j}\mu_{j}^{\ell}=K . For a fixed allocation, BMuon introduces a diagonal reweighting inside Muon’s spectral-norm constraint, with the components of the update variable corresponding to channel j j in block ℓ \ell weighted according to its allocation μ j ℓ \mu_{j}^{\ell} . BMuon chooses the allocation globally, intuitively asking where the update budget should be spent to obtain the greatest first-order decrease in the loss.

When trained from scratch, the architectures selected by BMuon- μ \mu outperform the nearly channel-matched uniform models in all four settings. Because both the discovered and uniform architectures are initialized from scratch and trained with standard Muon, this comparison isolates the effect of the architecture’s width profile. The results therefore provide evidence that BMuon- μ \mu identifies useful non-uniform architectures.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

Because both the discovered and uniform architectures are initialized from scratch and trained with standard Muon, this comparison isolates the effect of the architecture’s width profile. The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. passages.text: Training large language models (LLMs) entails a fundamental trade-off: memory-efficient optimizers such as Adam discard cross-parameter curvature, whereas full-curvature methods such as SOAP can accelerate convergence at prohibitive memory costs. We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

Methods marked ∗ ran out of memory, so their optimizer state is estimated. Training large language models (LLMs) forces a trade-off between memory and curvature. Adaptive optimizers store moment statistics that match or exceed the size of the model itself, and second-order methods such as Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) and SOAP ( Vyas et al., 2024 ) store even more. The remedies that reduce this footprint typically discard curvature information, producing poorly conditioned updates and slowing convergence ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) . Balancing memory efficiency with curvature fidelity has therefore emerged as a central challenge for efficient LLM training.

A range of optimizers have been proposed, each making a different trade-off between memory and curvature. First–order methods such as Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) and Adafactor ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) are lightweight optimizers that store only diagonal statistics. Their low memory cost makes them practical for large models. Full–matrix second–order methods such as Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) and KFAC ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) explicitly capture curvature and can accelerate training, but their quadratic state and computation make them prohibitive at LLMs scale. More recently, SOAP ( Vyas et al., 2024 ) achieved highly stable and full-rank preconditioning by applying Adam to the gradient projected onto the eigenbasis of Shampoo’s preconditioner; however, it still relies on explicitly accumulating full-rank covariance matrices. Several efficient optimizers have been proposed, but all of them have at least one optimizer memory state that grows quadratically with respect to model dimensions (i.e., 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n ) \mathcal{O}(mn) ) ( Romashov et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , making them difficult to scale. To resolve this, we introduce Clean , a curvature-aware optimizer that achieves SOAP-level performance while its memory states scale linearly with respect to model dimensions.

Clean’s memory advantage grows with scale (Figs. 7 and 8 ) because its memory complexity scales linearly with matrix dimensions, at a fixed rank r r , whereas every baseline carries at least one quadratic term (Table 2 ). Furthermore, Fig. 7 demonstrates a reduction in per-parameter memory cost as model size increases. See Appendix D for more details. (a) Validation loss against wall-clock time. (b) Token efficiency: Clean reaches that loss in 77 % 77\% of the training budget and Q-Clean in 87 % 87\% . To evaluate sample efficiency and convergence, Fig. 5 compares the methods across time and token budgets rather than focusing solely on the final loss. Clean reaches AdamW’s final performance in 64 hours instead of 81, while simultaneously reducing the optimizer memory footprint. It also only consumes 77% of the overall token budget, with Q-Clean requiring 87%.

Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

LLM pretraining is a computationally expensive stage of language-model development, where optimization quality, training time, and memory requirements jointly determine the models that can be trained within a given budget. The optimizer affects all three through its update rule, computational cost, and state storage. Therefore, improving optimization must be accompanied by efficient use of memory and hardware. AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) has long been the standard optimizer for large language models. Its coordinatewise updates are inexpensive and straightforward to shard across devices, but its first- and second-moment buffers account for a substantial share of training memory. GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , APOLLO ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and FRUGAL ( Zmushko et al., 2025 ) reduce this storage through compressed statistics or alternative update rules. Such savings can come at the cost of expensive projection operations or slower convergence, while leaving dense weights and gradients unchanged. Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) improves convergence by making an update geometry suited to matrix parameters, while also reducing optimizer state. It replaces coordinatewise adaptation with updates that approximately follow the polar factor of the momentum matrix, corresponding to spectral-norm steepest descent ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . The main cost of Muon is orthogonalization, which involves expensive matrix multiplications and, in sharded implementations, additional communication. Recent methods accelerate polar computation or modify the update and its distributed implementation ( Amsel et al., 2026a ; Khaled et al., 2025 ; Ahn et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . While these advances make matrix-aware updates cheaper, they retain dense weights and gradients.

The parameterization itself offers another route to efficiency. Reducing the number of trainable parameters reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer buffers together. For Muon, a suitable structure can also replace large orthogonalization problems with smaller ones. The important question is whether this computationally cheaper representation retains the optimization benefit of matrix-aware updates. Figure 1 : Training-step breakdown and optimizer-state memory for the 6.89B dense reference at microbatch 4 and four accumulation steps, from the same runs as Table 2 . Bars show median phase timings; labels give median full-step wall time. Periodic projection refreshes are excluded. Monarch–Muon uses four blocks and reduces both optimizer-state memory and optimizer-step overhead. We introduce Monarch–Muon, which parameterizes selected weights with Monarch factors ( Dao et al., 2022 ) and applies Muon directly to their trainable blocks. This representation uses fewer parameters while retaining the ability to express full-rank transformations, reducing storage for weights, gradients, and optimizer state. The smaller blocks also make Muon’s orthogonalization cheaper. In dense and mixture-of-experts pretraining, Muon improves validation loss over AdamW at fixed Monarch structure. Systems measurements show that the computational savings grow with matrix size, making the approach particularly effective at larger scales.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. Full-step measurements capture this crossover, which optimizer-step timings alone would miss. Table 2 : Training costs on one H100 at microbatch 4, indexed by the dense reference model size. 2610.04507:90b53b1e11a78b803e649deb5aa17.question: In the label-noise rank sweeps, how are LoRA and dense fine-tuning matched by modules, seeds, training budget, and parameter count, and what generalization results are reported for the 7B language model?

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

The shape, and where sweeps stop. Sweeping rank on an ImageNet-pretrained DeiT-Tiny under label noise, we find test risk minimized at r = 1 r{=}1 , climbing steeply exactly as ranks acquire the ability to fit the noisy labels, and peaking well below full rank. We call this shape the interpolation cliff (Figure 1 ). What matters for measuring the axis is where sweeps conventionally end. Stopped at full rank, the axis has undone 0.033 0.033 of the 0.531 0.531 nats the peak cost and reads as a flat plateau. When the sweep extends to 4 ​ d 4d , risk keeps descending. Whether a sweep sees the second descent depends on how far it is allowed to run (Section 3 ). Figure 1: Two shapes, and why the reference point decides between them. (a) On a from-scratch capacity axis, risk peaks at interpolation and then descends past its own pre-peak valley, the only reference such an axis has. (b) On an adapter’s rank axis a second reference exists, dense fine-tuning of the same modules. Parity, the rank at which the adapter has as many trainable weights as dense fine-tuning, arrives before r = d r{=}d , the smallest rank that can express every dense update, so the adapter stops saving parameters before it is as expressive as dense. Schematic; measurements in Figure 2 .

A protocol that sets the reference point. “How much of the peak was undone” has no answer without a reference, and this axis offers two that disagree. Grading the tail against the sweep’s own valley is what the double-descent literature does, because a from-scratch width sweep has no unrestricted counterpart to compare against. An adapter axis has one. The module-matched rank sweep (MMRS) runs the dial past full rank and grades every point against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules, sharing seeds, subsets and noise draws, with the trainable-parameter ratio reported beside every risk difference (Section 4 ). On this family the two references have room to disagree, because the window in which the adapter saves parameters closes at parity, r = 0.75 ​ d r{=}0.75d , before it can express every dense update at r = d r{=}d (Figure 1 b).

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.

passages.text: The 7 7 B rank axis is the clearest case for reading the tail against a module-matched baseline rather than against the pre-peak valley. Every sampled rank, parity included, remains behind dense in all three seeds, while the valley reference reads Rec > 1 \mathrm{Rec}>1 at every sampled rank from r = 448 r{=}448 on. Setup. Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) , with d = 3584 d{=}3584 and grouped-query attention with key and value width 512 512 , is fine-tuned for sequence classification on 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples ( Zhang et al., 2015 ) with 20 % 20\% symmetric label noise, sequence length 128 128 , a freshly initialized linear head, AdamW at lr 6.6 × 10 − 5 6.6\times 10^{-5} , weight decay 10 − 2 10^{-2} , batch 16 16 , 20 20 epochs, bfloat16. LoRA wraps the query, key and value projections of the last six blocks as three separate modules, so the adapter trains 15,360 ​ r 15{,}360r parameters per block against dense’s 16,515,072 16{,}515{,}072 and parity falls at r ≈ 1075 r{\approx}1075 . The dense arm trains the weights of those projections and freezes their biases, as does LoRA. Both arms train the same classification head with the same optimizer settings. Seeds control the subset, the noise draw, the head init and the adapter init, and are shared across arms, so the differences below are paired. Each run takes about an hour on one A100, and the r = 512 r{=}512 and r = 900 r{=}900 runs take under an hour each on one RTX 5090 under identical settings. 2610.20857:ee6c5305672053f215a7d756c502b.question: How were IDEA2PRIOR, ChatGPT Deep Research, and Gemini Deep Research evaluated for Hit@5, including query selection, relevance judgments, available evidence, and treatment of failures or missing papers?

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

2610.04249:efdc95dc6f3f631a11d2a58c3aae2.question: What balance and alignment assumptions underlie the singular-mode results for GD, Muon, Adam, Shampoo, and K-FAC, and what experiments, if any, test whether those results apply to neural-network or LLM weight spectra?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

We investigate these questions in deep linear networks, where depth changes the parameterization and optimization dynamics without changing the end-to-end linear functions. This makes it a particularly clean setting for separating optimizer-induced dynamics from parameterization-induced bias. Our theoretical analysis focuses on deep matrix factorization, a canonical special case in which the evolution of singular modes can be characterized explicitly. Specifically, in full observation regression, it exposes transient singular mode learning ( Saxe et al., 2013 ; Soudry et al., 2018 ) , while in underdetermined matrix sensing and completion, it permits direct study of which interpolating matrix is selected ( Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Rhee et al., 2026 ; Parviz et al., 2026 ) .

In contrast to the Euclidean geometry of GD, non-Euclidean optimizers transform the factorization-induced geometry in qualitatively different ways. SignGD and Adam apply coordinate-wise adaptive scaling ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) ; Muon acts directly on the spectrum of matrix updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) while Shampoo introduces history-dependent matrix preconditioning ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) ; and K-FAC attempts to compensate for the parameterization through curvature using approximate natural gradients ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) . In our study, we categorize these geometries based on their updates into Euclidean (GD), coordinate-wise (SignGD and Adam), spectral (Muon and Shampoo) and curvature based (K-FAC). These methods can reach nearly identical training losses while producing weights with different spectra, representations, and performance. Recent studies have begun to identify optimizer-dependent feature and simplicity biases, including differences between Adam and GD in nonlinear models ( Cattaneo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Xie and Li, 2024 ) and between spectral and Euclidean updates in deep linear networks ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) . These findings further motivate the central question we posed, and answering this requires distinguishing how quickly modes emerge from how they settle or disappear, since an optimizer can affect these phases differently. (a) GD (b) Muon (c) GD vs Muon: Birth and decay

Figure 1: Optimizer geometry sets the pace of spectral learning. In balanced aligned deep matrix factorization, GD and Muon produce distinct spectral learning trajectories (experimental details in App. F ). (a) Under GD, larger target modes are learned earlier, while smaller modes remain suppressed for longer. (b) Under Muon, factor amplitudes grow at a common speed, allowing smaller targets to reach full recovery earlier. (c) From the same initial amplitude 0.01 0.01 , Muon accelerates the growth of a positive target mode (red) and, importantly, removes the zero target mode in finite time (blue). GD instead exhibits delayed growth and slow decay. Thus, faster emergence of weak modes does not imply weaker removal of unsupported modes. Optimizer geometry determines which spectral components emerge, persist, and disappear. Other optimizers are discussed in later sections.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

passages.section: Implicit bias of Adam and related adaptive methods.
passages.text: Cattaneo et al. (2023) use backward error analysis to characterize corrections to Adam and RMSProp dynamics, relating implicit regularization to hyperparameters and training stage. The classification literature builds on the maximum margin characterization of GD for separable data ( Soudry et al., 2018 ) . Wang et al. (2021) study limiting parameter directions in homogeneous classification under their adaptive flow assumptions. Zhang et al. (2024) establish a maximum ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} margin result for full batch Adam in separable linear classification. Xie and Li (2024) connect AdamW, which includes decoupled weight decay, to ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} -norm constrained optimization under full-batch assumptions. Vasudeva et al. (2026) analyze a difference in feature learning between Adam and GD in a Gaussian classification model with two layer ReLU networks. These results concern distinct losses, optimizer conventions, or notions of bias. Our squared loss analysis studies finite singular amplitudes and phase times without weight decay, so classification margin results do not directly determine its birth or saturation laws.

(2024b) . In addition to standard performance metrics, we will examine other metrics more pertinent to the linear-algebraic structure of our weight and update matrices.
